transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-15 15:00 PT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood CSM), Jared Klein (Atlas Head of ML), Priya Rao (Eng Manager), Sam Ortiz (CTO), Maya Lin (Product)

[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intro, I'm Ava, AE for the account, Diego is our SE, Lena on CS. Jared, Priya, Sam, Maya, thanks for hopping on.
[01:12] Jared Klein: Yeah thanks. Real quick context - we're prototyping a chat assistant for merchants, mostly product recommendations and returns support. Current infra is a mix of on-prem models and calls to a public API, but we want to centralize. Key things for us: latency under 300ms for short flows, cost predictability, and tight data controls.
[02:05] Diego Martinez: Got it. Today we'll walk through the hosted API for chat/text generation basics - streaming, core params, and recommended retry patterns. We'll also show demo calls from our console.
[03:30] Priya Rao: One ask - when you talk latency, please call out cold-starts, and cache behavior, and how streaming affects perceived latency.
[04:05] Diego Martinez: Absolutely. Quick slide - hosted API is our easiest path: REST/SDK, streaming responses, and we support model pinning and fallbacks. For latency, we optimize kernel selection and batching on our end; for your 300ms SLOs we typically recommend a low-latency model family and prefix KV caching for session persistence.
[05:40] [Screen share starts - console shown] Diego Martinez: I'm going to call the chat endpoint now and show streaming. Watch the console - you should see token-by-token streaming.
[06:10] Speaker 2: uh oh, the console's a bit laggy on my end - ok i see it now.
[06:30] Diego Martinez: (typing) Here's a sample cURL: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>" -d '{"model":"rw-llm-lowlatency-1","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Recommend shoes for running"}],"stream":true}'
[07:05] Maya Lin: When you stream, do you charge per token as they stream?
[07:20] Ava Chen: Yes billing is per output token and embeddings units where applicable. Streaming doesn't change billing; it's just delivery.
[07:55] Diego Martinez: Note on perceived latency: streaming can start delivering partial tokens faster than waiting for full generation. So for short responses it often feels snappier. Also we can return early partial answers while continuing background tokens if you want to show progressive UI.
[09:10] Sam Ortiz: What about retries? If a request times out mid-stream, what's best practice?
[09:30] Diego Martinez: Good question. We recommend idempotency keys and deterministic request shaping. For short chat flows we suggest a small client-side timeout plus exponential backoff, and server-side we support resume tokens for some models - though not all. So pattern: (1) client sends idempotency-key, (2) if client sees network error, retry with same key using backoff, the service will either return stored response or regenerate based on policy.
[10:50] Jared Klein: Does the hosted API keep conversation state? We prefer storing state ourselves in our DB to control retention.
[11:10] Ava Chen: Hosted API supports stateless usage by you managing session state. We also offer optional session persistence with TTLs if you want Redwood-managed context caching; you can control retention via settings and audit logs.
[12:30] Priya Rao: For security - is the hosted option compatible with our VPC requirements?
[12:45] Ava Chen: Hosted by default is multi-tenant but data-in-transit and at-rest is encrypted, SOC 2 controls, and we can integrate with customer-managed KMS for key management. If you need a VPC-only private deployment, that's our Private offering, which runs in your VPC or on-prem. Many customers start hosted and move to Dedicated or Private as requirements tighten.
[14:00] Maya Lin: Any SLA differences between hosted and dedicated?
[14:12] Ava Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with a stronger SLA and reserved capacity for predictable latency. Hosted has a baseline SLA; for the kind of latency guarantees you mentioned, customers sometimes choose Dedicated or hybrid routing for critical endpoints.
[15:05] Diego Martinez: Back to the demo - I'm toggling temperature and max_tokens in the console. Lower temperature yields more deterministic answers; top_p is another knob for nucleus sampling. For recommendations we usually set temperature=0.2 and a token limit of ~80 for concise answers.
[16:30] [17:00] Speaker 1: (mumble) what's top p again?
[17:08] Diego Martinez: Top_p controls the cumulative probability mass of tokens to consider - it works with temperature to shape randomness. If you want deterministic outputs, use temperature 0 or very low and smaller top_p.
[18:40] Jared Klein: About cost - can you show unit economics? We have 10k users, 1.2 QPS peak per region, avg 30 tokens per response. What's the expected run-rate?
[19:10] Ava Chen: We'll follow up with a spreadsheet, but very roughly that maps to X tokens/month. We have committed use plans for hosted that reduce per-token cost; Dedicated gives better unit economics at higher commit levels. We'll send an example calc with your numbers.
[20:40] Diego Martinez: Quick note on batching: our runtime can batch requests to improve throughput, but batching increases tail latency for small synchronous calls. For low-latency merchant chat, you might prefer fewer batching windows.
[22:00] Priya Rao: Do you have SDKs for streaming? We use Node and Python.
[22:18] Diego Martinez: Yes Node and Python SDKs support streaming callbacks and event streams. We'll send sample repo links.
[23:05] Sam Ortiz: Any regulatory concerns with merchant PII? We need audit logs and deletion controls.
[23:28] Ava Chen: We have audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and retention controls. For sensitive PII some customers prefer Private deployments. We also support field-level redaction patterns and can integrate with DLP tooling.
[24:50] [25:15] Diego Martinez: I'm running a quick live latency test - calling the low-latency model 10x. Results: p50 ~120ms, p95 ~310ms in our hosted pop near their region (us-west). Remember numbers vary by prompt length and payload.
[26:40] Jared Klein: Those p95 numbers are close to our threshold; any levers to reduce p95 without moving to Dedicated?
[27:00] Diego Martinez: You can reduce p95 by shortening max_tokens, enforcing prompt templates to control sequence length, or use a smaller model tuned for latency. Also prefix caching helps if you have repeated system messages. Another tactic is regional routing to ensure requests hit nearest pop.
[28:30] Maya Lin: For the PoC, what's minimal work? We want to validate latency and basic correctness on our prompts.
[28:50] Ava Chen: Minimal PoC: you provide sample prompt set and dataset; we run benchmark script to reproduce latency and cost numbers; we optionally do a small integration with your staging keys. Diego will provide the script.
[30:00] Priya Rao: Timeline question - we need GA-ish decision in 6 weeks. Is that feasible?
[30:20] Ava Chen: Yes that's reasonable - PoC this week, results next week, then security review and procurement. The timeline aligns with committing to Dedicated if needed.
[31:05] [31:40] Speaker 3: (crosstalk) is there support for function calling or tool invocations?
[31:50] Diego Martinez: Yes we support structured outputs and tool calling patterns. For critical flows we'd pair you with an integration engineer.
[33:10] Jared Klein: One more nuance - retries may duplicate charges if a generation retriggers. How are you handling billing and duplication?
[33:35] Diego Martinez: With idempotency keys our system can detect retries and avoid double billing in many cases, but for non-idempotent regeneration there are semantics to consider. We'll document best practices; generally use idempotency and small backoffs.
[34:50] Ava Chen: Quick recap before we close. Action items: Diego sends benchmark script; Ava sends pricing and security docs; Jared to send sample prompts and QPS numbers; Priya to confirm PoC stakeholders. We plan to schedule kickoff on 2026-04-22 pending availability.
[36:20] Sam Ortiz: Also will need an NDA/contract review from procurement - we'll route that after pricing.
[37:00] Lena Park: We'll include our standard enterprise onboarding checklist in the follow-up.
[38:10] Priya Rao: One operational question - how do you surface token-level cost breakdowns?
[38:30] Ava Chen: In Redwood Console you can see per-request token breakdown, cost by route/model, and per-token analytics; we can export CSVs for finance.
[39:45] Maya Lin: Any gotchas with streaming and mobile clients?
[40:00] Diego Martinez: Mobile clients should handle partials and reconnect logic; SDKs have helpers for resuming streams. If network is flaky, use client timeouts and idempotency.
[41:30] Jared Klein: Ok this was helpful. We'll aim to get the prompt set to you by Monday.
[42:05] Ava Chen: Great thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items and a calendar invite for the PoC kickoff.
[43:12] [Call ends]
